newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks end modestly higher on election eve.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks end modestly higher on election eve.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks posted modest gains Monday as a plethora of mergers energised activity in individual shares, but most investors were cautious going into Tuesday's national elections.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 19.75 points at 6,041.68.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,331 to 1,040 on active volume of 391 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"The markets are doing well prior to the election on the assumption (President Bill) Clinton will be re-elected and we'll have nothing worse than a narrowing of the majority in Congress that Republicans will have," said Allen Sinai, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Global Economic Advisors.
Buyers also lifted bonds, with the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond up 7/32, which lowered its yield to 6.66 percent from 6.68 percent at Friday's close.
"The bond market is poised to do better if the elections turn out okay," said Sinai, who projects a modest selloff should the Democrats sweep and take both the White House and Congress.

Clinton's re-election was generally seen as a foregone conclusion, but Wall Street was still afraid that if the Democrats recapture the House and Senate from the Republicans, it would unleash a bearish market reaction because of their tax and spend policies.

"Bonds are concerned that a Democratic sweep will result in massive social spending and an upward explosion in the size of the deficit which will drive inflation higher and bond prices lower," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
Other than the elections, Wall Street also focused on the various big deals.
MCI Communications rose 1/2 to 30-3/4 on news that it would be acquired by British Telecommunications Plc for $20 billion -- the biggest trans-Atlantic deal ever.
Analysts said regulatory hurdles for the deal and a lengthy 12 months to complete it limited the rise in MCI's stock. British Telecom's American Depositary Shares surged 6-1/8 to 61-5/8.
AT&T lost 7/8 to 33-3/4 in the face of stronger competition from a merged MCI/BT.

Conrail Inc. fell 1-5/8 to 93-5/8 on news that its rival suitors CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp. were holding talks over their competing bids for Conrail, dampening hopes among Conrail shareholders that a protracted bidding war would emerge for the railroad.
Norfolk Southern rose 1-1/4 to 90-3/4 and CSX Corp. was up 1-7/8 to 44-7/8.
Southern National Corp. was off 1-3/4 to 33-1/2 and United Carolina Bancshares gained 8-1/2 to 36 after their boards approved a stock-swap merger valued at $985 million.
Sierra Health Services lost five at 23-7/8 on its merger with Physician Corp of America, which rose 1/8 to 10-3/4.
J.C. Penney Co. was down 1-7/8 at 51-1/8 and Eckerd Corp. gained 4-1/2 to 33-1/4 on the retailer's acquisition of the drugstore chain in a deal valued at $3.3 billion.

Among other individual shares, General Motors rose 1-5/8 to 55-5/8 as workers at a key metal stamping plant in Indianapolis returned to work after ratifying a deal to end a five-day strike that threatened to paralyse most of GM's light truck production.
Foster Wheeler lost 4-5/8 to 35-3/8 after warning that its 1997 results would fall short of its 15 percent annual growth goal.
The Nasdaq Composite index was off 1.30 points to 1,220.48.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 2.96 to 706.73. The American Stock Exchange index slipped 0.82 to 571.76.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.39 to 375.07. The average share was up 15 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 6,861.135 up 19.348 or 0.28 percent.
